title: Burst fingerprint hunting and WAF exception log
content:
TL;DR: Quick-hitting notes from on-call triage for a multi-vector traffic surge on 2026-02-14 that combined a leaked service token, client retries, and aggressive WAF rule hits. We mitigated with token revocation, temporary per-route soft quota, and WAF exceptions for validated client fingerprints. This doc is a working log + playbook fragment for hunting fingerprinted bursts and making short-lived WAF exceptions without opening a big attack surface.

High-level summary:
- Incident start: 2026-02-14 09:18 PST — sudden 8x baseline RPS on /v1/generate-chat and /v1/embeddings.
- Detection signal: alert "api-rate-spike-route" + increased 5xx from worker pool + spike in WAF rules: BOT_SIGNATURE_12 and SQLI-heuristic-2.
- Initial hypothesis: leaked service token (shared with low-priv dev env) being used by churned clients with naive retry logic. WAF started blocking some malformed payloads which caused partial failures and retries -> amplification.
- Impact: transient latency spikes (p95 doubled), increased cost (extra GPU time), user-facing 429/502 for some customers. No evidence of data exfil beyond request headers.

Timeline (notes to self / on-call):
- 09:20: Pager -> triage -> assigned (Ava)
- 09:24: Inspect logs: large number of distinct client_user_agent values but same Authorization token prefix and same truncated device_id header pattern.
- 09:30: Confirm token appears in multiple IPs across regions -> suspect public leak.
- 09:33: Create emergency JIRA SRE-4123 and post in #sre-ops slack; add token to emergency revoke list.
- 09:38: Revoke token, rotate keys for the small dev pool (manual via KMS console).
- 09:45: Apply temporary soft per-route quota: 50 rps aggregate for route group 'embeddings-heavy' (3 minute window) to reduce load while rollout continues.
- 09:47: Observed retries spike due to 429s from quota; identify noisy clients doing aggressive retry-backoff = 0.
- 09:50: Add WAF allowlist exception for signature BOT_SIGNATURE_12 for 10.10.0.0/16 (internal partner range) after verification.
- 10:10: System stabilized to ~1.2x baseline; latency P95 trending down but some 502s persist due to in-flight GPU tasks.
- 10:35: Opened follow-up tasks for dev teams to verify tokens, roll credentials, and add client-side backoff guidance.

Detection heuristics observed (for future automation):
- Token reuse across >5 regions in 2 minutes is high-fidelity indicator.
- Same Authorization prefix + high variance in user_agent but identical short device_id => fingerprint cluster.
- WAF rule churn combined with elevated retry count per IP (>30 retries/min) indicates amplifier.
- Sudden increase in KV cache misses for long prompt lengths suggests bots probing longer contexts.

Immediate mitigation checklist (what we did / maybe formalize into runbook steps):
1) Rapid token containment:
   - Identify top tokens by request volume (logstore query)
   - Add suspicious tokens to revocation list (KMS/Key service)
   - Notify SDK owners to rotate and patch examples that contain hardcoded tokens
2) Soft per-route throttles:
   - Apply conservative aggregate throttle per route group (not per-IP) to avoid splitting customers.
   - Use short TTL (3-10 minutes) and monitor for retry amplification.
3) WAF surgical exceptions:
   - For true positive internal or partner IP ranges, create temporary rule exceptions instead of disabling rule globally.
   - Add explicit allowlist entries with expiration timestamps and owner tags.
4) Circuit breakers for task queues:
   - When queue length > threshold and 5xx rates spike, stop accepting new long-running requests and return soft-fail (429) with diagnostic headers.
5) Communication:
   - Post to #sre-ops and @affected-customer contacts with status and ETA.

What worked:
- Fast revocation of compromised token dropped a large fraction of the malicious traffic.
- Short-lived per-route quota prevented cluster overload while preserving most latency-sensitive traffic.
- Surgical WAF exceptions reduced customer-facing false positives without re-opening the entire attack vector.

What hurt / surprises:
- Some clients had no backoff and retried immediately, causing retry storm after we added throttles -> created cascade.
- WAF rule names are opaque (BOT_SIGNATURE_12) and require manual mapping to criteria — slows triage.
- No automated pipeline to fingerprint tokens across regions (we ran ad-hoc queries).

Immediate follow-ups (owners, rough ETA):
- SRE: implement automated token reuse detector (SRE-4167) — owner: Liam Chen — ETA: 3 weeks.
- Product/Security: inventory all sample apps and passwordless keys in public repos; escalate to developer relations — owner: Sofia Gomez — ETA: 2 weeks.
- Infra: add more explicit WAF rule metadata in rule manager (human-friendly tags & description) — owner: Marcus Li — ETA: 4 weeks.
- DevX: publish SDK guidance for exponential backoff and default retry jitter — owner: Priya Nair — ETA: 1 week.

Playbook fragment: how to create a temporary WAF exception safely (rough draft):
- Preconditions: have the suspect IP range or fingerprint cluster and a slack approval from sec on-call.
- Steps:
  1) Add ephemeral allowlist entry scoped to IP/ASN or fingerprint hash; set TTL to 30m by default.
  2) Tag entry with owner and incident JIRA.
  3) Monitor error rates/customer tickets for 10 minutes. If error volume decreases and no new suspicious behaviors are observed, extend TTL to 2h; else revoke immediately.
  4) Record decision rationale in incident doc and schedule a rule-tuning follow-up.
- Danger notes: never whitelist a wide CIDR block unless it's a validated partner or internal network.

Telemetry improvements to avoid repeat: (low-hanging + midterm)
- Low-hanging: add token-prefix dimension to rate alerts, surface top-5 tokens in spike alert payload.
- Midterm: build fingerprint clustering pipeline to group requests by combination of token-prefix + device_id trunc + UA-similarity and surface cluster score.
- Longterm: tie fingerprint clusters to automated temporary throttles with human-in-loop approval for high-confidence clusters.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Were any customer credentials exposed in request bodies? Quick scan shows none but follow-up deeper scan needed (security).
- Should we default to per-IP or per-token throttles for hosted API? Per-token seems higher SNR but requires clean token hygiene.
- What's the acceptable TTL for WAF exceptions before we consider pushing a rule change? (propose: default 30m, escalate to 2h with CRO approval)

Notes to future on-call (conversational):
- If you see "token reused across regions" alert, prioritize token revocation over immediate global rule flips. Revocation plus soft throttles buys time.
- Be cautious with WAF blanket disables — it's easy to re-open an exploit. Think small: fingerprint or IP, not whole rule group.
- Watch for retry storm when throttles applied; if retries push latency back up, try circuit-breaker at ingress that returns small diagnostic JSON encouraging exponential backoff.

Appendix: useful ad-hoc queries (logstore pseudo-sql)
- top tokens last 10m: SELECT token_prefix, count(1) FROM requests WHERE ts > now() - interval '10 minutes' GROUP BY token_prefix ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 20;
- cluster fingerprint: SELECT substring(device_id,1,8) as devhash, user_agent_normalized, count(1) FROM requests WHERE token_prefix = 'tok_abc' AND ts > now()- interval '5 minutes' GROUP BY devhash, user_agent_normalized ORDER BY count DESC;

Links and refs: see linked artifacts above.

Status: doc is a working notes file; will formalize into runbook steps after SRE-4167 merges.

-- end of working log --
